pages.text: $(thing)FirmaLife HardCore$() has rewritten the cellar system. $(l)No Climate Station needed$() — the system automatically detects qualifying enclosed spaces.$(br2)Core principle: enclose an area with high $(l)thermal resistance$() blocks to reduce indoor temperature fluctuation. Indoor Temp = Base Temp + (Outdoor Temp − Base Temp) × (1 − Average Resistance).

pages.title: Thermal Resistance Tiers
pages.text: Blocks are categorized into three resistance tiers:$(br)$(li)$(thing)High (0.75)$(): Mud Bricks, Sealed Bricks, Sealed Brick Walls, Reinforced Soil$()$(br)$(li)$(thing)Medium (0.55)$(): Stone, Cobblestone, Rock Blocks, Dirt, Grass, Stone Bricks, Planks, Logs, Wattle, Support Beams, Obsidian$()$(br)$(li)$(thing)Low (0.25)$(): Glass, Glass Panes, Metal Blocks$()$(br2)Doors count as medium resistance. Double doors get a $(thing)4×$() multiplier.

pages.title: Preservation Tiers
pages.text: Lower effective temperature = better preservation:$(br)$(li)$(thing)SHELVED$(): ≤ 16°C, basic preservation$()$(br)$(li)$(thing)SHELVED_2$(): ≤ 8°C, moderate preservation$()$(br)$(li)$(thing)SHELVED_3$(): ≤ 0°C, optimal preservation$()$(br2)Spaces above 16°C provide no preservation. Build cellars in cold biomes for the best results.

pages.title: Building Tips
pages.text: $(li)Use high-resistance blocks (Sealed Bricks, Mud Bricks) for walls.$()$(br)$(li)Double doors are much more effective than single doors (4× bonus).$()$(br)$(li)Size limits: horizontal span ≤ 15 blocks, vertical ≤ 5 blocks.$()$(br)$(li)Place Food Shelves, Hangers, or Large Vessels inside after construction — they auto-receive preservation.$()$(br)$(li)Use a $(thing)Thermometer$()'s redstone signal to gauge indoor temperature.$()
